title: Type 2 Diabetes: Pick by the Patient

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction has a glycated hemoglobin (A1C) of 7.8% on metformin. Which is the best addition?
questions.explanation: C is correct: with heart failure, a sodium-glucose drug lowers sugar and keeps patients out of the hospital. A adds low-sugar risk without heart protection. B and D both carry heart failure warnings.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has an estimated kidney filtration rate (eGFR) of 40 and is not on metformin. Should metformin be started?

options.text: No, do not start metformin below 45
Yes, metformin is safe at any kidney function

questions.explanation: A is correct: do not start metformin below 45, and 40 is below 45. B and C ignore the kidney rule. D is wrong because food helps stomach upset, not the kidney limit.

questions.stem: A patient has taken metformin for years. Their eGFR has now fallen to 28. What is the best action?
questions.explanation: C is correct: stop metformin below 30, and 28 is below 30. A and D keep metformin past the stop point. B raises the dose when it should be stopped.

questions.stem: A patient starts dapagliflozin. Which counseling points are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genital yeast infections can occur, so teach hygiene
It commonly causes low blood sugar on its own
Ketoacidosis can occur even with near-normal sugar
Hold it when sick and not eating
Hold it at least 3 days before planned surgery

questions.explanation: A, C, D, and E are correct: genital yeast infections, rare ketoacidosis even with near-normal sugar, and holding the drug when sick and not eating or at least 3 days before surgery. B is wrong because the sodium-glucose drugs carry a low risk of low sugar on their own.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes wants semaglutide for diabetes and weight. Their mother had medullary thyroid cancer. What is the best action?

options.text: Start semaglutide at a low dose
Start semaglutide and check thyroid tests yearly
Do not start it; choose another option, such as a sodium-glucose drug

questions.explanation: D is correct: a family history of medullary thyroid cancer is a contraindication for every glucagon-like peptide one drug. A is wrong because a low dose does not remove the contraindication. B is wrong because tirzepatide carries the same contraindication. C still uses a contraindicated drug.

questions.stem: Which diabetes drugs can cause low blood sugar on their own? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: B, D, and F are correct: insulin and sulfonylureas like glyburide and glipizide can cause low blood sugar. A, metformin, C, semaglutide, and E, dapagliflozin, carry a low risk on their own; the risk rises when they are added to insulin or a sulfonylurea.

questions.stem: A patient on glipizide feels shaky. Fingerstick glucose is 62 mg/dL, and the patient is alert and swallowing normally. What is the best first step?

options.text: 15 grams of fast sugar, then recheck in 15 minutes

questions.explanation: A is correct: use the rule of 15: 15 grams of fast sugar, then recheck in 15 minutes. B is for a patient who cannot swallow safely, and this patient can. C makes low sugar worse. D, more glipizide, lowers sugar further.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease needs a drug chosen for protection. Which fits best?
questions.explanation: A is correct: for kidney disease, choose a sodium-glucose drug, or a glucagon-like peptide one agonist with proven kidney benefit. B adds low-sugar risk without protection. C causes fluid retention and carries a heart failure warning. D carries a heart failure warning and is not one of the protective choices taught.

questions.stem: Which long-term problem should be watched for with metformin?
questions.explanation: A is correct: metformin can cause long-term vitamin B12 deficiency. B is a sodium-glucose drug side effect. C is the boxed warning for glucagon-like peptide one drugs. D is wrong because metformin is not the drug linked to weight gain here.

questions.stem: Which effect helps semaglutide lower weight?

options.text: It sends sugar out in the urine
It blocks the liver's cholesterol enzyme
It slows the stomach and reduces hunger
It releases insulin even when the patient has not eaten

questions.explanation: C is correct: glucagon-like peptide one agonists slow the stomach and reduce hunger, so weight goes down. A describes the sodium-glucose drugs. B describes statins. D is wrong because these drugs release insulin when you eat.
